title: A gyroscope slung in a two-ring gimbal
abstract: A gyroscope slung in a two-ring gimbal.
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `base` **(static)** | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [0, 0, 0]`, `inverse_mass = 0` |
| `outer` | `torus` | `mass = 0.5`, `ring_radius = 0.9`, `tube_radius = 0.04`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `inner` | `torus` | `mass = 0.4`, `ring_radius = 0.7`, `tube_radius = 0.04`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `rotor` | `cylinder` | `mass = 2`, `radius = 0.5`, `half_height = 0.06`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`point`** — a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia. `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

**`torus`** — a uniform ring (a doughnut). `I_zz = m (c^2 + 3a^2/4)` about the axis of revolution and `I_xx = I_yy = m (c^2/2 + 5a^2/8)` about any diameter, for ring radius `c` and tube radius `a`. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, which is the axis of revolution — NOT a diameter. Getting those two confused makes a ring that spins invisibly instead of swinging. May also be given as `inner_radius`/`outer_radius`, which is the same ring described from the hole outward.

**`cylinder`** — a uniform solid cylinder. `I_zz = m r^2 / 2` about the axis of symmetry, and `I_xx = I_yy = m (3 r^2 + 4 h^2) / 12` about any diameter. Symmetric about its LOCAL z axis, like every round shape here. A long thin cylinder is a rod; a short fat one is a disc.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`inverse_mass`** — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.
- **`ring_radius`** — the distance from the torus centre to the middle of its tube.
- **`tube_radius`** — the radius of the torus tube itself.
- **`radius`** — the radius, in metres.
- **`half_height`** — half the height along the cylinder's own z axis.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is OFF** (`g_constant = 0`). The simulator's default is 1, so this had to be said explicitly; without it, bodies that are supposed only to bounce or to be held by joints would also attract each other.
- **Uniform gravity** is `[0, -3.0, 0]` metres per second squared, applied to every body alike.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
- **3 joints** hold the bodies together. A joint is an exact geometric relation held for all time by constraint forces the solver computes — not a stiff spring.
eom:
There are 4 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = m_i g + J^T lambda

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `m_i g` — the uniform field, here `g = [0, -3.0, 0]`
- `J^T lambda` — the constraint forces the joints generate. These are NOT written down by you: they are the Lagrange multipliers, solved for at every step so the joint equations hold exactly

and the torques `T_i` likewise carry a constraint part `J_omega^T lambda`, which is how a bearing resists being twisted out of line.
constraints:
**1. `hinge base outer [0, 1, 0]` — 5 rows.** The two bodies share a point and an axis: one freedom left, the swing. Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

**2. `hinge outer inner [1, 0, 0]` — 5 rows.** The two bodies share a point and an axis: one freedom left, the swing. Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

**3. `hinge inner rotor [0, 0, 1]` — 5 rows.** The two bodies share a point and an axis: one freedom left, the swing. Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

**The arithmetic that decides whether this can be solved at all.** 3 non-static bodies give `6 x 3 = 18` degrees of freedom, against **15 constraint rows**, leaving `18 - 15 = 3` freedoms.

Those remaining freedoms are the motion the mechanism actually has. Some of them may be passive — a freedom nothing applies a force along simply stays where it started.

Every row is held at the position level (`g = 0`) **and** at the velocity level (`d(g)/dt = J u = 0`) at the same time. That is what the GGL formulation is for, and it is why these joints do not slowly come apart.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 4 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
4 bodies x 13 numbers = 52 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

The 1 static body still occupies its 13 slots. Its inverse mass is zero, so its momentum-to-velocity map returns zero and it never moves — carried as constants rather than special-cased out of the layout.

On top of those 52 differential unknowns are the algebraic ones: one Lagrange multiplier `lambda` and one position-level multiplier `mu` for each of the 15 constraint rows, so

```
15 lambda + 15 mu = 30 algebraic unknowns
```

giving **82 unknowns in total**, solved as one implicit system.

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

Because there are joints this is a DAE, and `METHOD IDA` selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**. IDA is handed a residual of the implicit form

```
F(t, y, y') = 0
```

built from four blocks: the position rows carrying the `-M^-1 J^T mu` correction, the momentum rows carrying `+J^T lambda`, the rows `g(q) = 0`, and the rows `J u = 0`. IDA runs its variable-order variable-step BDF method and calls back into that residual; the Newton solve at each step is what determines the constraint forces.

**Tolerances.** This model has a joint that grips ORIENTATION, and such a joint imposes a floor of `rtol = 1e-6` and `atol = 1e-8` however tight a tolerance you ask for. That is not timidity: the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real, and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers. Every joint except `CONSTRAIN` grips orientation.

**Consistent start.** A DAE cannot start from an arbitrary state: the start must satisfy `g = 0` and `J u = 0` together. If the initial velocities are not compatible with the joints — a body turning about an offset pivot must have its centre moving — the simulator projects them onto the nearest compatible set and reports how much it changed them.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.g_constant = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -3.0, 0]` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `uniform_gravity` is a uniform gravitational field applied to every body, as `[gx, gy, gz]` in metres per second squared. This is the everyday 'g' of falling, entirely separate from the mutual attraction above.

The value expected here is `[0, -3.0, 0]`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`collide off` disarms contact detection. Nothing in this model is meant to touch anything else, so leaving it on would have the solver arm a rootfinder hunting for impacts that never happen. The form is `COLLIDE [ON|OFF]`; with no argument it reports the current setting.

It prints the resulting state and the number of collidable pairs.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 0")
sim.do("set system.uniform_gravity = [0, -3.0, 0]")
sim.do("collide off")

steps.title: Create the bodies
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> A POINT support: its inertia is the zero matrix, so it genuinely
> cannot turn. A sphere with inverse_mass = 0 would still be free to
> spin and the first hinge would drive it.

The next cell sends these 4 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

```
new <shape> [as <name>] { <field> = <value>, ... }
```

- `inverse_mass = 0` — one over the mass. Setting it to **0** makes the body STATIC: no force can accelerate it. This is how a body is bolted to the world, and it is representable as a finite number, which infinite mass is not.

Because `inverse_mass` is zero this body is **static**: no force can move it. It is part of the world, not part of the motion.

The command prints the name the simulator assigned, which is how you confirm the body exists.

steps.code:
sim.do("new point as base { mass = 1, position = [0, 0, 0], inverse_mass = 0 }")
sim.do("new torus as outer { mass = 0.5, ring_radius = 0.9, tube_radius = 0.04, position = [0, 0, 0] }")
sim.do("new torus as inner { mass = 0.4, ring_radius = 0.7, tube_radius = 0.04, position = [0, 0, 0] }")
sim.do("new cylinder as rotor { mass = 2, radius = 0.5, half_height = 0.06, position = [0, 0, 0] }")

steps.title: Create the bodies (2)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> A torus and a cylinder are both symmetric about their LOCAL z. A
> gimbal RING pivots about a DIAMETER, so each ring's plane has to
> contain two axes: the one it swings on, and the one it carries.
> outer swings on y, carries x  ->  plane xy  ->  symmetry axis z
> inner swings on x, carries z  ->  plane xz  ->  symmetry axis y
> so the outer ring needs no turn at all and the inner takes a quarter
> turn about x, as [w, x, y, z]. Face a ring's symmetry axis along the
> axis it swings on instead and "swinging" becomes a spin of a torus
> about its own axis of revolution: it neither shows nor does anything.
> The ROTOR is the opposite case and is meant to be that way — its
> symmetry axis IS its hinge axis, because that is what a rotor spins
> about — so it needs no turn either.

The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`set inner.orientation = [0.7071067811865476, 0.7071067811865476, 0, 0]` changes one property of the body `inner` after creation. `orientation` is the attitude, as a unit quaternion `[w, x, y, z]` — **w first**, everywhere in this simulator. Quaternions are used rather than Euler angles because they have no gimbal lock and renormalise cheaply. Setting it renormalises.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

steps.title: Declare the joints
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`HINGE` declares a joint. Its form is

```
HINGE <a> <b> <axis>
```

and it contributes **5 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 1 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share a point AND an axis: one freedom left, the swing.

Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

Here it is applied to `base outer [0, 1, 0]`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

---

`HINGE` declares a joint. Its form is

```
HINGE <a> <b> <axis>
```

and it contributes **5 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 1 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share a point AND an axis: one freedom left, the swing.

Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

Here it is applied to `outer inner [1, 0, 0]`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.

---

`HINGE` declares a joint. Its form is

```
HINGE <a> <b> <axis>
```

and it contributes **5 scalar constraint equations** to the system, leaving 1 of the 6 relative freedoms between the two bodies.

What it holds: the two bodies share a point AND an axis: one freedom left, the swing.

Three equations hold the shared point, exactly as a ball joint does. Two more hold the axis: taking `p` and `q` perpendicular to the hinge axis `h`, the rows are `p . (R_a h) = 0` and `q . (R_a h) = 0`, which say the axis carried by one body has not tipped away from the axis carried by the other.

Here it is applied to `inner rotor [0, 0, 1]`. The pivot goes at the **midpoint of the two bodies' centres as they stand right now**, and is then remembered in each body's own frame — which is why bodies are positioned before they are joined. The command prints a confirmation naming the joint and its row count.
steps.code:
sim.do("hinge base outer [0, 1, 0]")
sim.do("hinge outer inner [1, 0, 0]")
sim.do("hinge inner rotor [0, 0, 1]")

steps.title: Choose the integrator
steps.explain:
The next cell sends this command to the simulator. Here is exactly what it expects:

---

`method ida` chooses the time integrator. The form is `METHOD <adams|bdf|sprk|ida>`.

Here it selects the pure-Rust translation of **IDA**, SUNDIALS' implicit differential-algebraic solver. Any model with a joint MUST use it, and the simulator refuses every other method for such a model rather than silently integrating an unconstrained problem.

All stepping in this simulator goes through the vendored pure-Rust SUNDIALS translation. There is no hand-written Euler or Verlet anywhere.

steps.title: Create the bodies (3)
steps.explain:
**A note carried over from the example this notebook pairs with:**

> The start is a rigid rotation of the whole gimbal about the vertical,
> plus the rotor's own spin about its axis. Every hinge permits both, so
> g_dot = J u = 0 to roundoff and nothing is projected: the run begins
> on the constraint manifold.

The next cell sends these 3 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set outer.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 0]` changes one property of the body `outer` after creation. `angular_velocity` is the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set inner.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 0]` changes one property of the body `inner` after creation. `angular_velocity` is the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set rotor.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 15]` changes one property of the body `rotor` after creation. `angular_velocity` is the spin rate `omega`, as `[wx, wy, wz]` in radians per second, in WORLD axes. Setting it sets the angular momentum to `L = I omega`, which is what is carried.

Setters keep the coupled quantities consistent: setting a velocity updates the momentum, setting a mass updates the inverse mass, and setting an orientation renormalises the quaternion. A successful `set` prints nothing.
steps.code:
sim.do("set outer.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 0]")
sim.do("set inner.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 0]")
sim.do("set rotor.angular_velocity = [0, 1.0, 15]")

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- The values printed above are the result. Read them against the physical expectations set out earlier in this notebook.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

A gyroscope slung in a two-ring gimbal.

base --HINGE y-- outer ring --HINGE x-- inner ring --HINGE z-- rotor

Three hinges on three mutually perpendicular axes. A HINGE is 5 rows
and leaves one freedom, so three of them on three free bodies is

15 rows on 18 freedoms = 3 left

and those three are exactly the gimbal angles. Full rank, nothing
over-constrained, nothing locked.

EVERY BODY IS CONCENTRIC. Each joint pivots at the MIDPOINT of its
pair, so putting all four at the origin puts all three hinge axes
through one common point — which is what a gimbal is. The rings only
LOOK nested; their centres coincide exactly, and they stay coincident:
over the whole recording no centre moves further from the origin than
1.2e-34.

WHY GRAVITY DOES NOTHING HERE, unlike the spinning top. In that scene
the centre of mass hung a distance r from the pivot, so weight had a
lever arm and produced the precession. Here every centre of mass sits
ON the pivot. The lever arm is zero, so gravity exerts no torque at
all — the same `uniform_gravity` as the top recording, doing nothing.
A gimballed gyroscope is not holding itself up against gravity; it is
simply free.

TWO EXACT INVARIANTS, and both are worth watching for.

1. A hinge transmits no torque about its OWN axis — that is the
freedom it grants. The outermost hinge turns about the vertical,
so nothing can torque this system about the vertical, and the
total angular momentum along y is conserved:

L.y = 0.52688    held to 1.4e-14 over the whole run

2. The innermost hinge's axis IS the rotor's spin axis, so nothing can
torque the rotor about it either. Its axial spin is conserved:

I3 w3 = 0.25 * 15 = 3.75    held to 1 part in 100,000

WHAT TO WATCH. The whole assembly is started turning about the
vertical at 1 rad/s. A body with no gyroscope in it would simply keep
turning that way. This one does not: over 6.3 seconds the outer ring
never gets more than 7.43 degrees from where it began, and the
rotation put in comes back out as a TILT — the rotor's axis swings up
to 16.33 degrees away from its starting direction, at right angles to
the push. Rotation in about one axis, rotation out about another, is
the whole of gyroscopic behaviour.
